The FCIC report did not identify which of the 13 firms was not considered by Bernanke to be in danger of failure.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-145)

Economist [Mark Zandi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Zandi "Mark Zandi") testified to the [Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Crisis_Inquiry_Commission "Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission") in January 2010:

> The securitization markets also remain impaired, as investors anticipate more loan losses. Investors are also uncertain about coming legal and accounting rule changes and regulatory reforms. Private bond issuance of residential and commercial mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities, and CDOs peaked in 2006 at close to $2 trillion...In 2009, private issuance was less than $150 billion, and almost all of it was asset-backed issuance supported by the Federal Reserve's TALF program to aid credit card, auto and small-business lenders. Issuance of residential and commercial mortgage-backed securities and CDOs remains dormant.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-146)

_[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ reported in March 2010: "Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers were non-banks that were crippled by a silent run among panicky overnight "[repo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repo "Repo")" lenders, many of them money market funds uncertain about the quality of securitized collateral they were holding. Mass redemptions from these funds after Lehman's failure froze short-term funding for big firms."[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-147)

[![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Borrowing_Under_a_Securitization_Structure.png/500px-Borrowing_Under_a_Securitization_Structure.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Borrowing_Under_a_Securitization_Structure.png)

Borrowing under a [securitization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securitization "Securitization") structure

[Securitization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securitization "Securitization") – the bundling of bank loans to create [tradeable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_(financial_instrument) "Trade (financial instrument)")[bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_(finance) "Bond (finance)") – started in the mortgage industry in the 1970s, when Government Sponsored Enterprises (GSEs) began to pool relatively safe, conventional, "[conforming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conforming_loan "Conforming loan")" or "prime" mortgages, create "[mortgage-backed securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_securities "Mortgage-backed securities")" (MBS) from the pool, sell them to investors, guaranteeing these securities/bonds against default on the underlying mortgages.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn-26)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-148) This "originate-to-distribute" model had advantages over the old "originate-to-hold" model,[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC201189-149) where a bank originated a loan to the borrower/homeowner and retained the credit (default) risk. Securitization removed the loans from a bank's books, enabling the bank to remain in compliance with capital requirement laws. More loans could be made with proceeds of the MBS sale. The [liquidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_liquidity "Market liquidity") of a national and even international mortgage market allowed capital to flow where mortgages were in demand and funding short. However, securitization created a [moral hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard "Moral hazard") – the bank/institution making the loan no longer had to worry if the mortgage was paid off[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Devils-19-150) – giving them incentive to process mortgage transactions but not to ensure their credit quality.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-151)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-152) Bankers were no longer around to work out borrower problems and minimize defaults during the course of the mortgage.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-autogenerated1-153)

With the high [down payments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_payment "Down payment") and [credit scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_score_in_the_United_States "Credit score in the United States") of the conforming mortgages used by GSE, this danger was minimal.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-samuelson-154) Investment banks however, wanted to enter the market and avoid competing with the GSEs.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Devils-19-150) They did so by developing mortgage-backed securities in the riskier non-conforming subprime and [Alt-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-A "Alt-A") market. Unlike the GSEs[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-more-155) the issuers generally did not guarantee the securities against default of the underlying mortgages.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn-26)

What these "private label" or "non-agency" originators did do was to use "[structured finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structured_finance "Structured finance")" to create securities. Structuring involved "slicing" the pooled mortgages into "tranches", each having a different priority in the monthly or quarterly principal and interest stream.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC201170-9)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-tranch-156) Tranches were compared to "buckets" catching the "water" of principal and interest. More senior buckets did not share water with those below until they were filled to the brim and overflowing.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-157) This gave the top buckets/tranches considerable creditworthiness (in theory) that would earn the highest "triple A" credit ratings, making them sellable to [money market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_market_fund "Money market fund") and [pension funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension_fund "Pension fund") that would not otherwise deal with subprime mortgage securities.

[![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/CDO_-_FCIC_and_IMF_Diagram.png/500px-CDO_-_FCIC_and_IMF_Diagram.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CDO_-_FCIC_and_IMF_Diagram.png)

[IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF") diagram of [CDO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collateralized_debt_obligation "Collateralized debt obligation") and [RMBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residential_mortgage-backed_security "Residential mortgage-backed security")

To use up the MBS tranches lower in payback priority that could not be rated triple-A and that a conservative [fixed income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_income "Fixed income") market would not buy, investment banks developed another security – known as the [collateralized debt obligation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collateralized_debt_obligation "Collateralized debt obligation") (CDO). Although the CDO market was smaller, it was crucial because unless buyers were found for the non-triple-A or "[mezzanine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mezzanine_capital "Mezzanine capital")" tranches, it would not be profitable to make a mortgage-backed security in the first place.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-reckless-278-158)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-159) These CDOs pooled the leftover BBB, A−, etc. rated tranches, and produced new tranches – 70%[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-160) to 80%[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-161) of which were rated triple A by rating agencies. The 20–30% remaining mezzanine tranches were sometimes bought up by other CDOs, to make so-called "[CDO-Squared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDO-Squared "CDO-Squared")" securities which also produced tranches rated mostly triple A.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-162)

This process was later disparaged as "ratings laundering"[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-163) or a way of transforming "dross into gold"[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Endangerment-280-164) by some business journalists, but was justified at the time by the belief that home prices would always rise.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-165)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-166) The [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_model "Mathematical model") used by underwriters, rating agencies and investors to estimate the probability of mortgage default was based on the history of [credit default swaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_default_swaps "Credit default swaps"), which unfortunately went back "less than a decade, a period when house prices soared".[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-recipe-167)

In addition the model – which postulated that the correlation of default risks among loans in securitization pools could be measured in a simple, stable, tractable number, suitable for risk management or valuation[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-recipe-167) – also purported to show that the mortgages in CDO pools were well [diversified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversification_(finance) "Diversification (finance)") or "uncorrelated". Defaults on mortgages in [Orlando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida"), for example, were thought to have no effect on – i.e. were uncorrelated with – the real estate market across the country in [Laguna Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Beach "Laguna Beach"). When prices [corrected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_correction "Market correction") (i.e. the bubble collapsed), the resulting defaults were not only larger in number than predicted but far more correlated.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-recipe-167)

Still another innovative security criticized after the bubble burst was the [synthetic CDO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_CDO "Synthetic CDO"). Cheaper and easier to create than original "cash" CDOs, synthetics did not provide funding for housing, rather synthetic CDO-buying investors were in effect providing insurance (in the form of "credit default swaps") against mortgage default. The mortgages they insured were those in "cash" CDOs the synthetics "referenced". So instead of providing investors with interest and principal payments from MBS tranches, payments were the equivalent of [insurance premiums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_premium "Insurance premium") from the insurance "buyers".[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-168) If the referenced CDOs defaulted, investors lost their investment, which was paid out to the insurance buyers.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-169)

Unlike true insurance, credit default swaps were not regulated to insure that providers had the reserves to pay settlements, or that buyers owned the property (MBSs) they were insuring, i.e. were not simply making a bet a security would default.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC201150-170) Because synthetics "referenced" another (cash) CDO, more than one – in fact numerous – synthetics could be made to reference the same original, multiplying the effect if a referenced security defaulted.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-propublica.org-172) As with MBS and other CDOs, triple A ratings for "large chunks"[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-173) of synthetics were crucial to the securities' success, because of the buyer/investors' ignorance of the mortgage security market and trust in the credit rating agencies ratings.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-174)

Securitization began to take off in the mid-1990s. The total amount of mortgage-backed securities issued almost tripled between 1996 and 2007, to $7.3 trillion. The securitized share of subprime mortgages (i.e., those passed to third-party investors via MBS) increased from 54% in 2001, to 75% in 2006.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn.com-1020396-99) In the mid-2000s as the housing market was peaking, [GSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-sponsored_enterprise "Government-sponsored enterprise") securitization market share declined dramatically, while higher-risk [subprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime "Subprime") and [Alt-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-A "Alt-A") mortgage private label securitization grew sharply.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn-26) As mortgage defaults began to rise, it was among mortgages securitized by the [private banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_banks "Private banks"). GSE mortgages – securitized or not – continued to perform better than the rest of the market.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn-26)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-175) Picking up the slack for the dwindling cash CDO market[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011188-176) synthetics were the dominant form of CDO's by 2006,[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-greatest-177) valued "[notionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notional_amount "Notional amount")"[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-178) at an estimated $5 trillion.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-greatest-177)

By the autumn of 2008, when the securitization market "seized up" and investors would "no longer lend at any price", securitized lending made up about $10 trillion of the roughly $25 trillion American credit market, (i.e. what "American homeowners, consumers, and corporations owed").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Search_Site-143)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-brookings.edu-144) In February 2009, [Ben Bernanke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Bernanke "Ben Bernanke") stated that securitization markets remained effectively shut, with the exception of [conforming mortgages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conforming_loan "Conforming loan"), which could be sold to [Fannie Mae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fannie_Mae "Fannie Mae") and [Freddie Mac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mac "Freddie Mac").[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-179)

According to economist [A. Michael Spence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Michael_Spence "A. Michael Spence"): "when formerly uncorrelated risks shift and become highly correlated ... diversification models fail." "An important challenge going forward is to better understand these dynamics as the analytical underpinning of an early warning system with respect to financial instability."[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-viewpoints1-180)

Criticizing the argument that complex structured investment securitization was instrumental in the mortgage crisis, [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman") points out that the Wall Street firms issuing the securities "kept the riskiest assets on their own books", and that neither of the equally disastrous bubbles in European housing or US commercial property used complex structured securities. Krugman does agree that it is "arguable is that financial innovation ... spread the bust to financial institutions around the world" and its inherent fragmentation of loans has made post-bubble "cleanup" through debt renegotiation extremely difficult.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-slump-140)

#### Financial institution debt levels and incentives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Financial institution debt levels and incentives")]

[![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Leverage_ratios_for_major_investment_banks.svg/500px-Leverage_ratios_for_major_investment_banks.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leverage_ratios_for_major_investment_banks.svg)

[Leverage ratios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverage_ratio "Leverage ratio") of [investment banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_banks "Investment banks") increased significantly between 2003 and 2007.

The [Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Crisis_Inquiry_Commission "Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission") reported in January 2011 that: "From 1978 to 2007, the amount of debt held by the financial sector soared from $3 trillion to $36 trillion, more than doubling as a share of gross domestic product. The very nature of many Wall Street firms changed – from relatively staid private partnerships to publicly traded corporations taking greater and more diverse kinds of risks. By 2005, the 10 largest U.S. commercial banks held 55% of the industry's assets, more than double the level held in 1990. On the eve of the crisis in 2006, financial sector profits constituted 27% of all corporate profits in the United States, up from 15% in 1980."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011-2)

Many [financial institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_institutions "Financial institutions"), [investment banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_bank "Investment bank") in particular, issued large amounts of debt during 2004–07, and invested the proceeds in [mortgage-backed securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_securities "Mortgage-backed securities") (MBS), essentially betting that house prices would continue to rise, and that households would continue to make their mortgage payments. Borrowing at a lower interest rate and investing the proceeds at a higher interest rate is a form of [financial leverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_leverage "Financial leverage"). This is analogous to an individual taking out a second mortgage on his residence to invest in the stock market. This strategy proved profitable during the housing boom, but resulted in large losses when house prices began to decline and mortgages began to default. Beginning in 2007, financial institutions and individual investors holding MBS also suffered significant losses from mortgage payment defaults and the resulting decline in the value of MBS.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-BlackburnSMC1-181)

A 2004 [U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") (SEC) decision related to the [net capital rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_capital_rule "Net capital rule") allowed US investment banks to issue substantially more debt, which was then used to purchase MBS. Over 2004–07, the top five US investment banks each significantly increased their financial leverage (see diagram), which increased their vulnerability to the declining value of MBSs. These five institutions reported over $4.1 trillion in debt for fiscal year 2007, about 30% of US nominal GDP for 2007. Further, the percentage of subprime mortgages originated to total originations increased from below 10% in 2001–03 to between 18–20% from 2004 to 2006, due in-part to financing from investment banks.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-blogspot1-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-publications2-115)

During 2008, three of the largest U.S. investment banks either went bankrupt ([Lehman Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehman_Brothers "Lehman Brothers")) or were sold at fire sale prices to other banks ([Bear Stearns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Stearns "Bear Stearns") and [Merrill Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_Lynch "Merrill Lynch")). These failures augmented the instability in the [global financial system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_financial_system "Global financial system"). The remaining two investment banks, [Morgan Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley") and [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"), opted to become commercial banks, thereby subjecting themselves to more stringent regulation.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-182)[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-183)

In the years leading up to the crisis, the top four U.S. depository banks moved an estimated $5.2 trillion in assets and liabilities [off-balance sheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-balance_sheet "Off-balance sheet") into [special purpose vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_purpose_vehicles "Special purpose vehicles") or other entities in the [shadow banking system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_banking_system "Shadow banking system"). This enabled them to essentially bypass existing regulations regarding minimum capital ratios, thereby increasing leverage and profits during the boom but increasing losses during the crisis. New accounting guidance will require them to put some of these assets back onto their books during 2009, which will significantly reduce their capital ratios. One news agency estimated this amount to be between $500 billion and $1 trillion. This effect was considered as part of the stress tests performed by the government during 2009.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-184)

[Martin Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Wolf "Martin Wolf") wrote in June 2009: "...an enormous part of what banks did in the early part of this decade – the off-balance-sheet vehicles, the derivatives and the 'shadow banking system' itself – was to find a way round regulation."[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-185)

The New York State Comptroller's Office has said that in 2006, Wall Street executives took home bonuses totaling $23.9 billion (~$35.7 billion in 2024). "Wall Street traders were thinking of the bonus at the end of the year, not the long-term health of their firm. The whole system – from mortgage brokers to Wall Street risk managers – seemed tilted toward taking short-term risks while ignoring long-term obligations. The most damning evidence is that most of the people at the top of the banks didn't really understand how those [investments] worked."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-businessweek1-61)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-186)

The incentive compensation of traders was focused on fees generated from assembling financial products, rather than the performance of those products and profits generated over time. Their bonuses were heavily skewed towards cash rather than stock and not subject to "[claw-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clawback "Clawback")" (recovery of the bonus from the employee by the firm) in the event the MBS or CDO created did not perform. In addition, the increased risk (in the form of financial leverage) taken by the major investment banks was not adequately factored into the compensation of senior executives.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-187)

#### Credit default swaps

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Credit default swaps")]

[Credit default swaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_default_swaps "Credit default swaps") (CDS) are financial instruments used as a hedge and protection for debtholders, in particular MBS investors, from the risk of default, or by speculators to profit from default. As the net worth of banks and other financial institutions deteriorated because of losses related to subprime mortgages, the likelihood increased that those providing the protection would have to pay their counterparties. This created uncertainty across the system, as investors wondered which companies would be required to pay to cover mortgage defaults.

Like all [swaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swap_(finance) "Swap (finance)") and other [financial derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_derivatives "Financial derivatives"), CDS may either be used to [hedge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_(finance) "Hedge (finance)") risks (specifically, to insure creditors against default) or to profit from speculation. The volume of CDS outstanding increased 100-fold from 1998 to 2008, with estimates of the debt covered by CDS contracts, as of November 2008, ranging from US$33 to $47 trillion.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-188):73 CDS are lightly regulated, largely because of the [Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity_Futures_Modernization_Act_of_2000 "Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000"). As of 2008, there was no central [clearing house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearing_house_(finance) "Clearing house (finance)") to honor CDS in the event a party to a CDS proved unable to perform his obligations under the CDS contract. Required disclosure of CDS-related obligations has been criticized as inadequate. Insurance companies such as [American International Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Group "American International Group") (AIG), [MBIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBIA "MBIA"), and [Ambac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambac "Ambac") faced ratings downgrades because widespread mortgage defaults increased their potential exposure to CDS losses. These firms had to obtain additional funds (capital) to offset this exposure. AIG's having CDSs insuring $440 billion of MBS resulted in its seeking and obtaining a Federal government bailout.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-189) The monoline insurance companies went out of business in 2008–2009.

When investment bank [Lehman Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehman_Brothers "Lehman Brothers") went bankrupt in September 2008, there was much uncertainty as to which financial firms would be required to honor the CDS contracts on its $600 billion (~$856 billion in 2024) of bonds outstanding.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-190)[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-191)[Merrill Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_Lynch "Merrill Lynch")'s large losses in 2008 were attributed in part to the drop in value of its unhedged portfolio of [collateralized debt obligations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collateralized_debt_obligation "Collateralized debt obligation") (CDOs) after [AIG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIG "AIG") ceased offering CDS on Merrill's CDOs. The loss of confidence of trading partners in Merrill Lynch's solvency and its ability to refinance its [short-term debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-term_debt "Short-term debt") led to its acquisition by the [Bank of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_America "Bank of America").[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-NYT-Morgenson-2008-11-08-192)[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Bloomberg-Paulden-2008-08-26-193)

Economist [Joseph Stiglitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz "Joseph Stiglitz") summarized how credit default swaps contributed to the systemic meltdown: "With this complicated intertwining of bets of great magnitude, no one could be sure of the financial position of anyone else-or even of one's own position. Not surprisingly, the credit markets froze."[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-194)

Author [Michael Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Lewis "Michael Lewis") wrote that CDS enabled speculators to stack bets on the same mortgage bonds and CDO's. This is analogous to allowing many persons to buy insurance on the same house. Speculators that bought CDS insurance were betting that significant defaults would occur, while the sellers (such as [AIG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIG "AIG")) bet they would not. A theoretically infinite amount could be wagered on the same housing-related securities, provided buyers and sellers of the CDS could be found.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-195)

Derivatives such as CDS were unregulated or barely regulated. Several sources have noted the failure of the US government to supervise or even require transparency of the [financial instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_instruments "Financial instruments") known as [derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative_(finance) "Derivative (finance)").[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-196)[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-devils-197)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-faiola-198) A 2008 investigative article in _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ found that leading government officials at the time (Federal Reserve Board Chairman [Alan Greenspan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Greenspan "Alan Greenspan"), Treasury Secretary [Robert Rubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rubin "Robert Rubin"), and [SEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") Chairman [Arthur Levitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Levitt "Arthur Levitt")) vehemently opposed any regulation of derivatives. In 1998 [Brooksley E. Born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooksley_E._Born "Brooksley E. Born"), head of the [Commodity Futures Trading Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity_Futures_Trading_Commission "Commodity Futures Trading Commission"), put forth a policy paper asking for feedback from regulators, lobbyists, legislators on the question of whether derivatives should be reported, sold through a central facility, or whether capital requirements should be required of their buyers. Greenspan, Rubin, and Levitt pressured her to withdraw the paper and Greenspan persuaded [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") to pass a resolution preventing CFTC from regulating derivatives for another six months – when Born's term of office would expire.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-devils-197) Ultimately, it was the collapse of a specific kind of derivative, the [mortgage-backed security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_security "Mortgage-backed security"), that triggered the economic crisis of 2008.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-faiola-198)

In addition, Chicago Public Radio, Huffington Post, and ProPublica reported in April 2010 that market participants, including a hedge fund called [Magnetar Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetar_Capital "Magnetar Capital"), encouraged the creation of CDO's containing low quality mortgages, so they could bet against them using CDS. NPR reported that Magnetar encouraged investors to purchase CDO's while simultaneously betting against them, without disclosing the latter bet.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-propublica.org-172)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-199)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-200) Instruments called [synthetic CDO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_CDO "Synthetic CDO"), which are portfolios of credit default swaps, were also involved in allegations by the SEC against Goldman-Sachs in April 2010.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-201)

The [Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Crisis_Inquiry_Commission "Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission") reported in January 2011 that CDS contributed significantly to the crisis. Companies were able to sell protection to investors against the default of mortgage-backed securities, helping to launch and expand the market for new, complex instruments such as CDO's. This further fueled the housing bubble. They also amplified the losses from the collapse of the housing bubble by allowing multiple bets on the same securities and helped spread these bets throughout the financial system. Companies selling protection, such as [AIG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIG "AIG"), were not required to set aside sufficient capital to cover their obligations when significant defaults occurred. Because many CDS were not traded on exchanges, the obligations of key financial institutions became hard to measure, creating uncertainty in the financial system.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011-2)

#### Inaccurate credit ratings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Inaccurate credit ratings")]

[![Image 18](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/MBS_Downgrades_Chart.png/500px-MBS_Downgrades_Chart.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBS_Downgrades_Chart.png)

[MBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_security "Mortgage-backed security") credit rating downgrades, by quarter

Credit rating agencies – firms which rate debt [instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_instrument "Financial instrument")/[securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securities "Securities") according to the debtor's ability to pay lenders back – have come under scrutiny during and after the financial crisis for having given investment-grade ratings to MBSs and CDOs based on risky subprime mortgage loans that later defaulted. Dozens of lawsuits have been filed by investors against the "[Big Three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Three_(credit_rating_agencies) "Big Three (credit rating agencies)")" rating agencies – [Moody's Investors Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody's_Investors_Service "Moody's Investors Service"), [Standard & Poor's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_&_Poor's "Standard & Poor's") and [Fitch Ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitch_Ratings "Fitch Ratings").[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-dozens-202) The [Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Crisis_Inquiry_Commission "Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission") (FCIC) concluded the "failures" of the Big Three rating agencies were "essential cogs in the wheel of financial destruction" and "key enablers of the financial meltdown".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011-2) Economist [Joseph Stiglitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz "Joseph Stiglitz") called them "one of the key culprits" of the financial crisis.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-203) Others called their ratings "catastrophically misleading", (the [U.S. Securities and Exchange Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission")[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-casey-204)), their performance "horrendous" (_[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ magazine[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-econ-205)). There are indications that some involved in rating subprime-related securities knew at the time that the rating process was faulty.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-206)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-207)

The position of the three agencies "between the issuers and the investors of securities"[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC201143%E2%80%9344-208) "transformed" them into "key" players in the housing bubble and financial crisis according to the _Financial Crisis Inquiry Report_. Most investors in the fixed income market had no experience with the mortgage business – let alone dealing with the complexity of pools of mortgages and tranche priority of MBS and CDO securities – and were simply looking for an independent party who could rate securities.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC201144-209) The putatively independent parties meanwhile were paid "handsome fees" by investment banks "to obtain the desired ratings", according to one expert.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC201144-209)

In addition, a large section of the debt securities market – many [money markets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_market_fund "Money market fund") and [pension funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pension_fund "Pension fund") – were restricted in their bylaws to holding only the safest securities – i.e securities the rating agencies designated "triple-A". Hence non-prime securities could not be sold without ratings by (usually two of) the three agencies.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-McLean_p.111-210)

From 2000 to 2007, one of the largest agencies – Moody's – rated nearly 45,000 mortgage-related securities[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-nber-211) – more than half of those it rated – as triple-A.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011xxv-212) By December 2008, there were over $11 (~$16.00 in 2024) trillion structured finance securities outstanding in the U.S. bond market debt.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-nber-211) But as the boom matured, mortgage underwriting standards deteriorated. By 2007 an estimated $3.2 (~$4.65 trillion in 2024) trillion in loans were made to homebuyers and owners with bad credit and undocumented incomes, bundled into MBSs and CDOs, and given top ratings[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-loose-213) to appeal to global investors.

As these mortgages began to default, the three agencies were compelled to go back and redo their ratings. Between autumn of 2007 and the middle of 2008, agencies downgraded nearly $2 trillion in MBS tranches.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-214) By the end of 2008, 80% of the CDOs by value[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-215) rated "triple-A" were downgraded to junk.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011224;229-216) Bank writedowns and losses on these investments totaled $523 billion.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-loose-213)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-scourge-gold-217)[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-bottom-218)

Critics such as the FCIC argue the mistaken credit ratings stemmed from "flawed computer models, the pressure from financial firms that paid for the ratings, the relentless drive for market share, the lack of resources to do the job despite record profits, and the absence of meaningful public oversight".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011-2)

Structured investment was very profitable to the agencies and by 2007 accounted for just under half of Moody's total ratings revenue and all of the revenue growth.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-219) But profits were not guaranteed, and issuers played the agencies off one another, 'shopping' around to find the best ratings, sometimes openly threatening to cut off business after insufficiently generous ratings.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-shopping-220) Thus there was a conflict of interest between accommodating clients – for whom higher ratings meant higher earnings – and accurately rating the debt for the benefit of the debt buyer/investors – who provided zero revenue to the agencies.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-221)

Despite the profitability of the three big credit agencies – Moody's operating margins were consistently over 50%, higher than famously successful [ExxonMobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExxonMobil "ExxonMobil") or [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft")[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-222) – salaries and bonuses for non-management were significantly lower than at Wall Street banks, and its employees complained of overwork.

This incentivized agency rating analysts to seek employment at those Wall Street banks who were issuing mortgage securities, and who were particularly interested in the analysts' knowledge of what criteria their former employers used to rate securities.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-223)[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011193-224) Inside knowledge of interest to security issuers eager to find loopholes included the fact that rating agencies looked at the _average_ credit score of a pool of borrowers, but not how dispersed it was; that agencies ignored borrower's household income or length of credit history (explaining the large numbers of low income immigrants given mortgages—people "who had never failed to repay a debt, because they had never been given a loan"); that agencies were indifferent to credit worthiness issues of [adjustable-rate mortgages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjustable-rate_mortgage "Adjustable-rate mortgage") with low teaser rates, "silent second" mortgages, or [no-documentation mortgages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_doc_loan#In_United_States "No doc loan").[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-short-225)

As of 2010, virtually all of the investigations of rating agencies, criminal as well as civil, are in their early stages.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-226) In New York, state prosecutors are examining whether eight banks[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-227) duped the credit ratings agencies into inflating the grades of subprime-linked investments.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-story-228) In the dozens of suits filed against them by investors involving claims of inaccurate ratings[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-dozens-202) the rating agencies have defended themselves using the [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment "First Amendment") defense—that a credit rating is an opinion protected as free speech.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-nagy-229) In 2013, McClatchy Newspapers found that "little competition has emerged" since the Credit Rating Agency Reform Act of 2006 was passed "in rating the kinds of complex home-mortgage securities whose implosion led to the 2007 financial crisis". The Big Three's market share of outstanding credit rating has barely shrunk, moving from 98% to 97%.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-gordon-230)

### Governmental policies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Governmental policies")]

Government over-regulation, failed regulation and deregulation have all been claimed as causes of the crisis. Increasing home ownership has been the goal of several presidents including Roosevelt, Reagan, Clinton and [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-231)

#### Decreased regulation of financial institutions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Decreased regulation of financial institutions")]

> Those of us who have looked to the self-interest of lending institutions to protect shareholders' equity, myself included, are in a state of shocked disbelief.

Several steps were taken to [deregulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deregulate "Deregulate") banking institutions in the years leading up to the crisis. Further, major investment banks which collapsed during the crisis were not subject to the regulations applied to depository banks. In testimony before Congress both the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "Securities and Exchange Commission") (SEC) and [Alan Greenspan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Greenspan "Alan Greenspan") claimed failure in allowing the self-regulation of investment banks.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-233)[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-234)

In 1982, Congress passed the [Alternative Mortgage Transactions Parity Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_Mortgage_Transaction_Parity_Act_of_1982 "Alternative Mortgage Transaction Parity Act of 1982") (AMTPA), which allowed non-federally chartered housing creditors to write adjustable-rate mortgages. This bi-partisan legislation was, according to the Urban Institute, intended to "increase the volume of loan products that reduced the up-front costs to borrowers in order to make homeownership more affordable."[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-235) Among the new mortgage loan types created and gaining in popularity in the early 1980s were adjustable-rate, option adjustable-rate, balloon-payment and interest-only mortgages. Subsequent widespread abuses of predatory lending occurred with the use of adjustable-rate mortgages.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-The_downturn_in_facts_and_figures-34)[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-236) Approximately 90% of subprime mortgages issued in 2006 were adjustable-rate mortgages.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Zandi_2010-12)

The [Glass–Steagall Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass%E2%80%93Steagall_Act "Glass–Steagall Act") was enacted after the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"). It separated [commercial banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_bank "Commercial bank") and [investment banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_bank "Investment bank"), in part to avoid potential conflicts of interest between the lending activities of the former and rating activities of the latter. In 1999 Glass–Steagall was repealed by the [Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramm-Leach-Bliley_Act "Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act"). Economist [Joseph Stiglitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz "Joseph Stiglitz") criticized the repeal of Glass–Steagall because, in his opinion, it enabled the risk-taking culture of investment banking to dominate the more conservative commercial banking culture, leading to increased levels of risk-taking and leverage during the boom period.[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-vanityfair.com-237) President Bill Clinton, who signed the legislation, dismissed its connection to the subprime mortgage crisis, stating (in 2008): "I don't see that signing that bill had anything to do with the current crisis."[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-238)

The [Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity_Futures_Modernization_Act_of_2000 "Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000") was bi-partisan legislation that formally exempted [derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative_(finance) "Derivative (finance)") from regulation, supervision, trading on established exchanges, and capital reserve requirements for major participants. It "provided a legal safe harbor for treatment already in effect."[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-239) Concerns that counterparties to derivative deals would be unable to pay their obligations caused pervasive uncertainty during the crisis. Particularly relevant to the crisis are [credit default swaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_default_swaps "Credit default swaps") (CDS), a derivative in which Party A pays Party B what is essentially an insurance premium, in exchange for payment should Party C default on its obligations. [Warren Buffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Buffett "Warren Buffett") famously referred to derivatives as "financial weapons of mass destruction" in early 2003.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-240)[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-241)

Former Fed Chair [Alan Greenspan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Greenspan "Alan Greenspan"), who many economists blamed for the financial crisis, testified in October 2008 that he had trusted free markets to self-correct and had not anticipated the risk of reduced lending standards."Those of us who have looked to the self-interest of lending institutions to protect shareholders' equity, myself included, are in a state of shocked disbelief."[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Greenspan_2008-232)

Some analysts believe the subprime mortgage crisis was due, in part, to a 2004 decision of the SEC that affected 5 large investment banks. The critics believe that changes in the [capital reserve calculation rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_capital_rule "Net capital rule") enabled investment banks to substantially increase the level of debt they were taking on, fueling the growth in mortgage-backed securities supporting subprime mortgages. These banks dramatically increased their risk taking from 2003 to 2007. By the end of 2007, the largest five U.S. investment banks had over $4 (~$5.81 trillion in 2024) trillion in debt with high ratios of debt to equity, meaning only a small decline in the value of their assets would render them insolvent.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Labaton-242)[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-NYTS-243) However, in an April 9, 2009, speech, Erik Sirri, then director of the SEC's Division of Trading and Markets, argued that the regulatory weaknesses in leverage restrictions originated in the late 1970s: "The Commission did not undo any leverage restrictions in 2004," nor did it intend to make a substantial reduction.[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Fried257-244)

The financial sector invested heavily to gain clout in the halls of government to bring about these major deregulatory objectives: it spent more than $5 billion over a decade to strengthen its political clout in Washington, DC, including $1.725 billion in political [campaign contributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_contribution "Campaign contribution") and $3.4 billion on [Industry lobbyists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industry_lobbyist "Industry lobbyist") during the years 1998–2008.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-245)

#### Policies to promote private ownership of housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Policies to promote private ownership of housing")]

> "Members of the Right tried to blame the seeming market failures on government; in their mind the government effort to push people with low incomes into home ownership was the source of the problem. Widespread as this belief has become in conservative circles, virtually all serious attempts to evaluate the evidence have concluded that there is little merit in this view."

Several administrations, both Democratic and Republican, advocated private home ownership in the years leading up to the crisis. The [Housing and Community Development Act of 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_and_Community_Development_Act_of_1992 "Housing and Community Development Act of 1992") established, for the first time, a mandate to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac for loans to enable home ownership of less expensive housing, a mandate to be regulated by the [Department of Housing and Urban Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Housing_and_Urban_Development "Department of Housing and Urban Development") (HUD). Initially, the 1992 legislation required that 30% or more of Fannie's and Freddie's loan purchases be in support of private home ownership of affordable housing. However, HUD was given the power to set future requirements. During the later part of the [Clinton administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton_administration "Clinton administration"), HUD Secretary [Andrew Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cuomo "Andrew Cuomo") announced "new regulations to provide $2.4 trillion in mortgages for affordable housing for 28.1 million families, which increased the required percentage of mortgage loans for low- and moderate-income families that finance companies Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac must buy annually from the then current 42% of their total purchases to a new high of 50%.[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-247) Eventually (under the Bush administration) a 56% minimum was established.[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-248) Additionally, in 2003, "The Bush administration today recommended the most significant regulatory overhaul in the housing finance industry since the savings and loan crisis a decade ago."[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-249)

"The National Homeownership Strategy: Partners in the American Dream", was compiled in 1995 by Henry Cisneros, President Clinton's HUD Secretary. This 100-page document represented the viewpoints of HUD, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, leaders of the housing industry, various banks, numerous activist organizations such as [ACORN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Community_Organizations_for_Reform_Now "Association of Community Organizations for Reform Now") and [La Raza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_of_La_Raza "National Council of La Raza"), and representatives from several state and local governments."[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-250) In 2001, the independent research company, Graham Fisher & Company, stated: "While the underlying initiatives of the [strategy] were broad in content, the main theme … was the relaxation of credit standards."[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-251)

The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission (majority report), Federal Reserve economists, and several academic researchers have stated that government affordable housing policies were not the major cause of the financial crisis.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn-26)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Regulation_and_the_Mortgage_Crisis-117) They also state that Community Reinvestment Act loans outperformed other "subprime" mortgages, and [GSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-sponsored_enterprise "Government-sponsored enterprise") mortgages performed better than private label securitizations.

The [Community Reinvestment Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Reinvestment_Act "Community Reinvestment Act") (CRA) was originally enacted under President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") in 1977 in an effort to encourage banks to halt the practice of lending discrimination.[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-252) In 1995 the Clinton administration issued regulations that added numerical guidelines, urged lending flexibility, and instructed bank examiners to evaluate a bank's responsiveness to community activists (such as [ACORN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Community_Organizations_for_Reform_Now "Association of Community Organizations for Reform Now")) when deciding whether to approve bank merger or expansion requests.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-fragile-253) Critics claim that the 1995 changes to CRA signaled to banks that relaxed lending standards were appropriate and could minimize potential risk of governmental sanctions.

In its "Conclusions" submitted January 2011, the [Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Crisis_Inquiry_Commission "Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission") reported that

> "the CRA was not a significant factor in subprime lending or the crisis. Many subprime lenders were not subject to the CRA. Research indicates only 6% of high-cost loans—a proxy for subprime loans—had any connection to the law. Loans made by CRA-regulated lenders in the neighborhoods in which they were required to lend were half as likely to default as similar loans made in the same neighborhoods by independent mortgage originators not subject to the law."[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011xxvii-254)

Critics claim that the use of the high-interest-rate proxy distorts results because government programs generally promote low-interest rate loans—even when the loans are to borrowers who are clearly subprime.[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-255) However, several economists maintain that Community Reinvestment Act loans outperformed other "subprime" mortgages, and GSE mortgages performed better than private label securitizations.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-ssrn-26)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Regulation_and_the_Mortgage_Crisis-117)

However, economists at the [National Bureau of Economic Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Economic_Research "National Bureau of Economic Research") (NBER) concluded that banks undergoing CRA-related regulatory exams took additional mortgage lending risk. The authors of a study entitled "Did the Community Reinvestment Act Lead to Risky Lending?" found that "in the six quarters surrounding a CRA exam, lending by banks undergoing a CRA exam is 5 percent higher on average". They concluded: "The evidence shows that around CRA examinations, when incentives to conform to CRA standards are particularly high, banks not only increase lending rates but also appear to originate loans that are markedly riskier." Loan delinquency averaged 15% higher in the treatment group than the control group one year after mortgage origination.[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-256)

#### State and local governmental programs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: State and local governmental programs")]

As part of the 1995 National Homeownership Strategy, HUD advocated greater involvement of state and local organizations in the promotion of affordable housing.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-257) In addition, it promoted the use of low or no-down payment loans and second, unsecured loans to the borrower to pay their down payments (if any) and closing costs.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-258) This idea manifested itself in "silent second" loans that became extremely popular in several states such as California, and in scores of cities such as San Francisco.[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-259) Using federal funds and their own funds, these states and cities offered borrowers loans that would defray the cost of the down payment. The loans were called "silent" because the primary lender was not supposed to know about them. A Neighborhood Reinvestment Corporation (affiliated with HUD) publicity sheet explicitly described the desired secrecy: "[The NRC affiliates] hold the second mortgages. Instead of going to the family, the monthly voucher is paid to [the NRC affiliates]. In this way the voucher is "invisible" to the traditional lender and the family (emphasis added)[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-260)

### Role of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Role of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac")]

[Fannie Mae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fannie_Mae "Fannie Mae") and [Freddie Mac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mac "Freddie Mac") are [government-sponsored enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-sponsored_enterprise "Government-sponsored enterprise") (GSE) that purchase mortgages, buy and sell [mortgage-backed securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_securities "Mortgage-backed securities") (MBS), and guarantee nearly half of the mortgages in the U.S. A variety of political and competitive pressures resulted in the GSEs ramping up their purchase and guarantee of risky mortgages in 2005 and 2006, just as the housing market was peaking.[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011xxvi-261)[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-262) Fannie and Freddie were both under political pressure to expand purchases of higher-risk affordable housing mortgage types, and under significant competitive pressure from large investment banks and mortgage lenders.[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Duhigg-263)

As early as February 2004, in testimony before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, Alan Greenspan (chairman of the Federal Reserve) raised serious concerns regarding the [systemic financial risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systemic_risk "Systemic risk") that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac represented. He implored Congress to take actions to avert a crisis.[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-264) The GSEs dispute these studies and dismissed Greenspan's testimony.

Nine of the ten members of the [Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Crisis_Inquiry_Commission "Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission") reported in 2011 that Fannie and Freddie "contributed to the crisis, but were not a primary cause",[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011xxvi-261) or that since "credit spreads declined not just for housing, but also for other asset classes like commercial real estate ... problems with U.S. housing policy or markets [could] not by themselves explain the U.S. housing bubble."[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-GOP-265) According to the Commission, GSE mortgage securities essentially maintained their value throughout the crisis and did not contribute to the significant financial firm losses that were central to the financial crisis. The GSEs participated in the expansion of subprime and other risky mortgages, but they followed rather than led Wall Street and other lenders into subprime lending.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011-2)

Several studies by the [Government Accountability Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Accountability_Office "Government Accountability Office") (GAO), Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, the [Federal Housing Finance Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Housing_Finance_Agency "Federal Housing Finance Agency"), and several academic institutions summarized by economist Mike Konczal of the [Roosevelt Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Institute "Roosevelt Institute"), indicate Fannie and Freddie were not to blame for the crisis.[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-266) A 2011 statistical comparisons of regions of the US which were subject to GSE regulations with regions that were not, done by the [Federal Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve "Federal Reserve"), found that GSEs played no significant role in the subprime crisis.[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-267) In 2008, David Goldstein and Kevin G. Hall reported that more than 84% of the subprime mortgages came from private lending institutions in 2006, and the share of subprime loans insured by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac decreased as the bubble got bigger (from a high of insuring 48% to insuring 24% of all subprime loans in 2006).[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Mcclatchy-268) In 2008, another source found estimates by some analysts that Fannie's share of the subprime mortgage-backed securities market dropped from a peak of 44% in 2003 to 22% in 2005, before rising to 33% in 2007.[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Duhigg-263)

Whether GSEs played a small role in the crisis because they were legally barred from engaging in subprime lending is disputed.[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-NYT-Fanny,_Freddie_and_You-269) Economist [Russell Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Roberts "Russell Roberts")[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-270) cites a June 2008 _[Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Post "Washington Post")_ article which stated that "[f]rom 2004 to 2006, the two [GSEs] purchased $434 billion in securities backed by subprime loans, creating a market for more such lending."[[271]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-271) Furthermore, a 2004 HUD report admitted that while trading securities that were backed by subprime mortgages was something that the GSEs officially disavowed, they nevertheless participated in the market.[[272]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-272)

Insofar as Fannie and Freddie did purchase substandard loans, some analysts question whether government mandates for affordable housing were the motivation. In December 2011 the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "Securities and Exchange Commission") charged the former Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives, accusing them of misleading investors about risks of subprime-mortgage loans and about the amount of subprime mortgage loans they held in portfolio.[[273]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-273) According to financial analyst [Karen Petrou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Shaw_Petrou "Karen Shaw Petrou"), "The SEC's facts paint a picture in which it wasn't high-minded government mandates that did the GSEs wrong, but rather the monomaniacal focus of top management on marketshare. With marketshare came bonuses and with bonuses came risk-taking, understood or not."[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-274) However, there is evidence suggesting that governmental housing policies were a motivational factor. Daniel H. Mudd, the former CEO of Fannie Mae, stated: "We were afraid that lenders would be selling products we weren't buying and Congress would feel like we weren't fulfilling our mission." Another senior Fannie Mae executive stated: "Everybody understood that we were now buying loans that we would have previously rejected, and that the models were telling us that we were charging way too little, but our mandate was to stay relevant and to serve low-income borrowers. So that's what we did."[[275]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-autogenerated2-275)

In his lone dissent to the majority and minority opinions of the FCIC, [Peter J. Wallison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_J._Wallison "Peter J. Wallison") of the [American Enterprise Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Enterprise_Institute "American Enterprise Institute") (AEI) blamed U.S. housing policy, including the actions of Fannie and Freddie, primarily for the crisis, writing: "When the bubble began to deflate in mid-2007, the low quality and high risk loans engendered by government policies failed in unprecedented numbers. The effect of these defaults was exacerbated by the fact that few if any investors – including housing market analysts – understood at the time that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac had been acquiring large numbers of subprime and other high risk loans in order to meet HUD's affordable housing goals." His dissent relied heavily on the research of fellow AEI member Edward Pinto, the former Chief Credit Officer of Fannie Mae. Pinto estimated that by early 2008 there were 27 million higher-risk, "non-traditional" mortgages (defined as subprime and Alt-A) outstanding valued at $4.6 (~$6.56 trillion in 2024) trillion. Of these, Fannie & Freddie held or guaranteed 12 million mortgages valued at $1.8 trillion. Government entities held or guaranteed 19.2 million or $2.7 trillion of such mortgages total.[[276]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-276)

One counter-argument to Wallison and Pinto's analysis is that the credit bubble was global and also affected the U.S. commercial real estate market, a scope beyond U.S. government housing policy pressures. The three Republican authors of the dissenting report to the FCIC majority opinion wrote in January 2011: "Credit spreads declined not just for housing, but also for other asset classes like commercial real estate. This tells us to look to the credit bubble as an essential cause of the U.S. housing bubble. It also tells us that problems with U.S. housing policy or markets do not by themselves explain the U.S. housing bubble."[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011415-277) Economist Paul Krugman wrote in January 2010 that Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, CRA, or predatory lending were not primary causes of the bubble/bust in residential real estate because there was a bubble of similar magnitude in commercial real estate in America.[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-278)

Countering the analysis of Krugman and members of the FCIC, Peter Wallison argues that the crisis was caused by the bursting of a real estate bubble that was _supported largely by low or no-down-payment loans_, which was uniquely the case for U.S. _residential_ housing loans. He states: "It is not true that every bubble – even a large bubble – has the potential to cause a financial crisis when it deflates." As an example, Wallison notes that other developed countries had "large bubbles during the 1997–2007 period" but "the losses associated with mortgage delinquencies and defaults when these bubbles deflated were far lower than the losses suffered in the United States when the 1997–2007 [bubble] deflated."[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-aei.org-279)

Other analysis calls into question the validity of comparing the residential loan crisis to the commercial loan crisis. After researching the default of commercial loans during the financial crisis, Xudong An and Anthony B. Sanders reported (in December 2010): "We find limited evidence that substantial deterioration in CMBS [commercial mortgage-backed securities] loan underwriting occurred prior to the crisis."[[280]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-280) Other analysts support the contention that the crisis in commercial real estate and related lending took place _after_ the crisis in residential real estate. Business journalist Kimberly Amadeo wrote "The first signs of decline in residential real estate occurred in 2006. Three years later, commercial real estate started feeling the effects."[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-281) Denice A. Gierach, a real estate attorney and CPA, wrote:

> ...most of the commercial real estate loans were good loans destroyed by a really bad economy. In other words, the borrowers did not cause the loans to go bad, it was the economy.[[282]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-282)

A second counter-argument to Wallison's dissent is that the definition of "non-traditional mortgages" used in Pinto's analysis overstated the number of risky mortgages in the system by including Alt-A, which was not necessarily high-risk. Krugman explained in July 2011 that the data provided by Pinto significantly overstated the number of subprime loans, citing the work of economist Mike Konczal: "As Konczal says, all of this stuff relies on a form of [three-card monte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-card_monte "Three-card monte"): you talk about 'subprime and other high-risk' loans, lumping subprime with other loans that are not, it turns out, anywhere near as risky as actual subprime; then use this essentially fake aggregate to make it seem as if Fannie/Freddie were actually at the core of the problem."[[283]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-283)

### Other contributing factors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Other contributing factors")]

#### Policies of central banks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Policies of central banks")]

[![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Fed_Funds_Rate_%26_Mortgage_Rates_2001_to_2008.png/500px-Fed_Funds_Rate_%26_Mortgage_Rates_2001_to_2008.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fed_Funds_Rate_&_Mortgage_Rates_2001_to_2008.png)

[Federal funds rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate "Federal funds rate") and various [mortgage rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage_rates "Mortgage rates")

[Central banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") manage monetary policy and may target the rate of inflation. They have some authority over [commercial banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_bank "Commercial bank") and possibly other financial institutions. They are less concerned with avoiding asset [price bubbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_bubble "Price bubble"), such as the [housing bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_bubble "Housing bubble") and [dot-com bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble "Dot-com bubble"). Central banks have generally chosen to react after such bubbles burst so as to minimize collateral damage to the economy, rather than trying to prevent or stop the bubble itself. This is because identifying an asset bubble and determining the proper monetary policy to deflate it are matters of debate among economists.[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-WallStreetJournal-284)[[285]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-285)

Some market observers have been concerned that [Federal Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve "Federal Reserve") actions could give rise to [moral hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard "Moral hazard").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-brown1-36) A [Government Accountability Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Accountability_Office "Government Accountability Office") critic said that the [Federal Reserve Bank of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Bank_of_New_York "Federal Reserve Bank of New York")'s rescue of [Long-Term Capital Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-Term_Capital_Management "Long-Term Capital Management") in 1998 would encourage large financial institutions to believe that the Federal Reserve would intervene on their behalf if risky loans went sour because they were "[too big to fail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too_big_to_fail "Too big to fail")."[[286]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-286)

A contributing factor to the rise in house prices was the Federal Reserve's lowering of interest rates early in the decade. From 2000 to 2003, the Federal Reserve lowered the [federal funds rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate "Federal funds rate") target from 6.5% to 1.0%.[[287]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-287) This was done to soften the effects of the collapse of the [dot-com bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble "Dot-com bubble") and of the [September 2001 terrorist attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"), and to combat the perceived risk of [deflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deflation "Deflation").[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-WallStreetJournal-284)

The Fed believed that interest rates could be lowered safely primarily because the rate of inflation was low; it disregarded other important factors. According to Richard W.
