Fisher, President and CEO of the [Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Bank_of_Dallas "Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas"), the Fed's interest rate policy during the early 2000s (decade) was misguided, because measured inflation in those years was below true inflation, which led to a monetary policy that contributed to the housing bubble.[[288]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-288)

[Ben Bernanke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Bernanke "Ben Bernanke") and Alan Greenspan — both former chairmen of the Federal Reserve — disagree, arguing decisions on purchasing a home depends on long-term interest rates on mortgages not the short-term rates controlled by the Fed. According to Greenspan, "between 1971 and 2002, the fed funds rate and the mortgage rate moved in lock-step," but when the Fed started to raise rates in 2004,[[289]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-289)[[290]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-290)[[291]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-291) mortgage rates diverged, continuing to fall (or at least not rise) for another year (see "Fed Funds Rate & Mortgage Rates" graph). Construction of new homes did not peak until January 2006.[[292]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFCIC2011103-292) Bernanke speculates that a world wide "saving glut" pushed capital or savings into the United States, keeping long-term interest rates low and independent of Central Bank action.[[293]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Bernanke-293)

Agreeing with Fisher that the low interest rate policy of the Greenspan Fed both allowed and motivated investors to seek out risk investments offering higher returns, is finance economist [Raghuram Rajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raghuram_Rajan "Raghuram Rajan") who argues that the underlying causes of the American economy's tendency to go "from bubble to bubble" fueled by unsustainable monetary stimulation, are the "weak safety nets" for the unemployed, which made "the US political system ... acutely sensitive to job growth";[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-KOEHN-294) and attempts to compensate for the stagnant income of the middle and lower classes with easy credit to boost their consumption.[[295]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Campbell-295)

Economist [Thomas Sowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sowell "Thomas Sowell") wrote that the Fed's decision to steadily raise interest rates was a key factor that ended the housing bubble. The Fed raised rates from the unusually low level of 1% in 2004 to a more typical 5.25% in 2006. By driving mortgage rates higher, the Fed "made monthly mortgage payments more expensive and therefore reduced the demand for housing." He referred to the Fed action as the "nudge" that collapsed the "house of cards" created by lax lending standards, affordable housing policies, and the preceding period of low interest rates.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Sowell_2009-52)

#### Mark-to-market accounting rule

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Mark-to-market accounting rule")]

Former [Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Deposit_Insurance_Corporation "Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation") Chair William Isaac placed much of the blame for the subprime mortgage crisis on the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "Securities and Exchange Commission") and its fair-value accounting rules, especially the requirement for banks to mark their assets to market, particularly mortgage-backed securities.[[296]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-296) Whether or not this is true has been the subject of ongoing debate.[[297]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-297)[[298]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-298)

The debate arises because this accounting rule requires companies to adjust the value of marketable securities (such as the [mortgage-backed securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_securities "Mortgage-backed securities") (MBS) at the center of the crisis) to their market value. The intent of the standard is to help investors understand the value of these assets at a point in time, rather than just their historical purchase price. Because the market for these assets is distressed, it is difficult to sell many MBS at other than prices which may (or may not) be reflective of market stresses, which may be below the value that the mortgage cash flow related to the MBS would merit. As initially interpreted by companies and their auditors, the typically lower sale value was used as the market value rather than the cash flow value. Many large financial institutions recognized significant losses during 2007 and 2008 as a result of marking-down MBS asset prices to market value.[[299]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-299)

#### Globalization, technology and the trade deficit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Globalization, technology and the trade deficit")]

[![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/U.S._Trade_Deficit_2011.png/500px-U.S._Trade_Deficit_2011.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U.S._Trade_Deficit_2011.png)

U.S. [current account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_account_(balance_of_payments) "Current account (balance of payments)") or [trade deficit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_deficit "Trade deficit") through 2012

In 2005, [Ben Bernanke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Bernanke "Ben Bernanke") addressed the implications of the United States's high and rising [current account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_account_(balance_of_payments) "Current account (balance of payments)") deficit, resulting from U.S. investment exceeding its savings, or imports exceeding exports.[[300]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-300) Between 1996 and 2004, the U.S. current account deficit increased by $650 billion, from 1.5% to 5.8% of GDP. The U.S. attracted a great deal of foreign investment, mainly from the emerging economies in Asia and oil-exporting nations. The [balance of payments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_of_payments "Balance of payments")[identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_(mathematics) "Identity (mathematics)") requires that a country (such as the U.S.) running a [current account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_account_(balance_of_payments) "Current account (balance of payments)") deficit also have a [capital account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_account "Capital account") (investment) surplus of the same amount. Foreign investors had these funds to lend, either because they had very high personal savings rates (as high as 40% in China), or because of high oil prices.

Bernanke referred to this as a "[saving glut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saving_glut "Saving glut")"[[293]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Bernanke-293) that may have _pushed_ capital into the United States, a view differing from that of some other economists, who view such capital as having been _pulled_ into the U.S. by its high consumption levels. In other words, a nation cannot consume more than its income unless it sells assets to foreigners, or foreigners are willing to lend to it. Alternatively, if a nation wishes to increase domestic investment in plant and equipment, it will also increase its level of imports to maintain balance if it has a floating exchange rate.

Regardless of the push or pull view, a "flood" of funds ([capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_capital "Financial capital") or [liquidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquidity "Liquidity")) reached the U.S. financial market. Foreign governments supplied funds by purchasing [U.S. Treasury bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Treasury_bonds "U.S. Treasury bonds") and thus avoided much of the direct impact of the crisis. American households, on the other hand, used funds borrowed from foreigners to finance consumption or to bid up the prices of housing and financial assets. Financial institutions invested foreign funds in mortgage-backed securities. American housing and financial assets dramatically declined in value after the housing bubble burst.[[301]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-301)[[302]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-302)

Economist [Joseph Stiglitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz "Joseph Stiglitz") wrote in October 2011 that the recession and high unemployment of the 2009–2011 period was years in the making and driven by: unsustainable consumption; high manufacturing productivity outpacing demand thereby increasing unemployment; income inequality that shifted income from those who tended to spend it (i.e., the middle class) to those who do not (i.e., the wealthy); and emerging market's buildup of reserves (to the tune of $7.6 trillion by 2011) which was not spent. These factors all led to a "massive" shortfall in aggregate demand, which was "papered over" by demand related to the housing bubble until it burst.[[303]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-303)

## Subprime mortgage crisis phases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Subprime mortgage crisis phases")]

### January 2007 to March 2008

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: January 2007 to March 2008")]

[![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Securitization_Market_Activity.png/500px-Securitization_Market_Activity.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Securitization_Market_Activity.png)

Securitization markets were impaired during the crisis.

Financial market stresses became apparent during 2007 that resulted in sizable losses across the financial system, the bankruptcy of over 100 mortgage lenders and the emergency sale of investment bank [Bear Stearns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Stearns "Bear Stearns") in March 2008 to depository bank [JP Morgan Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JP_Morgan_Chase "JP Morgan Chase"). Some writers began referring to the events in the financial markets during this period the "Subprime Mortgage Crisis" or the "Mortgage crisis".[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-BlackburnSMC1-181)[[304]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-NYTBear1-304)

As U.S. housing prices began to fall from their 2006 peak, global investors became less willing to invest in [mortgage-backed securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_securities "Mortgage-backed securities") (MBS). The crisis began to affect the financial sector in February 2007, when [HSBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSBC "HSBC"), one of the world's largest banks, said its charge for bad debts would be $10.5 billion (~$15.3 billion in 2024), 20% higher than expectations. The increase was driven by increased expected losses in its US mortgage portfolio; this was the first major subprime related loss to be reported.[[305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-305)[[306]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-306) By April 2007, over 50 mortgage companies had declared bankruptcy, many of which had specialized in subprime mortgages, the largest of which was [New Century Financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Century_Financial "New Century Financial").[[307]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-WaPoNewCentury-307) At least 100 [mortgage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage_law "Mortgage law") companies either shut down, suspended operations or were sold during 2007.[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-bloomberg1-308) These mortgage companies made money on the origination and sale of mortgages, rather than interest from holding the mortgage. They had relied on continuing access to this global pool of investor capital to continue their operations; when investor capital dried-up, they were forced into bankruptcy.

Other parts of the [shadow banking system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_banking_system "Shadow banking system") also encountered difficulty. Legal entities known as [structured investment vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structured_investment_vehicle "Structured investment vehicle") (SIV) and [hedge funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_fund "Hedge fund") had borrowed from investors and bought MBS's. When mortgage defaults rose along with the fall in housing prices, the value of the MBS declined. Investors demanded that these entities put up additional collateral or be forced to pay back the investors immediately, a form of [margin call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margin_call "Margin call"). This resulted in further sales of MBS, which lowered MBS prices further. This dynamic of margin call and price reductions contributed to the collapse of two Bear Stearns hedge funds in July 2007, an event which economist [Mark Zandi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Zandi "Mark Zandi") referred to as "arguably the proximate catalyst" of the crisis in financial markets.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Zandi_2010-12) On August 9, 2007, French bank [BNP Paribas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BNP_Paribas "BNP Paribas") announced that it was halting redemptions on three investment funds due to subprime problems, another "beginning point" of the crisis to some observers.[[309]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-309)[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-310)

Investment banks such as Bear Stearns had legal obligations to provide financial support to these entities, which created a cash drain. Bear Stearns reported the first quarterly loss in its history during November 2007 and obtained additional financing from a Chinese [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund"). Investment banks Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley had also obtained additional capital from sovereign wealth funds in Asia and the Middle East during late 2007.[[304]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-NYTBear1-304)

The major investment banks had also increased their own borrowing and investing as the bubble expanded, taking on additional risk in the search for profit. For example, as of November 30, 2006, Bear Stearns reported $383.6 billion in liabilities and $11.8 billion in equity, a leverage ratio of approximately 33.[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-311) This high leverage ratio meant that only a 3% reduction in the value of its assets would render it insolvent. Unable to withstand the combination of high leverage, reduced access to capital, loss in the value of its MBS securities portfolio, and claims from its hedge funds, Bear Stearns collapsed during March 2008. Historian [Robin Blackburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Blackburn "Robin Blackburn") wrote: "The Wall Street investment banks and brokerages hemorrhaged $175 billion of capital in the period July 2007 to March 2008, and Bear Stearns, the fifth largest, was 'rescued' in March, at a fire-sale price, by JP Morgan Chase with the help of $29 billion of guarantees from the Federal Reserve."[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-BlackburnSMC1-181)

### April to December 2008

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Subprime_mortgage_crisis&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: April to December 2008")]

[![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/TED_Spread_graph_%282006%E2%80%932010%29.svg/500px-TED_Spread_graph_%282006%E2%80%932010%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TED_Spread_graph_(2006%E2%80%932010).svg)

The [TED spread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TED_spread "TED spread"), an indicator of [credit risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_risk "Credit risk"), increased dramatically during September 2008.

Financial market conditions continued to worsen during 2008. Simultaneously, the price of oil had been rising steadily since mid-2007 from an already high value (100$) to a peak of 191$ in June 2008, which exacerbated market woes.[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-312) By August 2008, [financial firms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_firms "Financial firms") around the globe had [written down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Write_down "Write down") their holdings of subprime related securities by US$501 billion (~$715 billion in 2024).[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-313) The IMF estimated that financial institutions around the globe would eventually have to write off $1.5 trillion of their holdings of subprime MBSs. About $750 billion in such losses had been recognized as of November 2008. These losses wiped out much of the capital of the world banking system. Banks headquartered in nations that have signed the [Basel Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basel_Accords "Basel Accords") are required to maintain a ratio of [liquid capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_requirement "Capital requirement") for every dollar of credit extended to consumers and businesses. Thus the massive reduction in bank capital just described has reduced the credit available to businesses and households.[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-foreignaffairs1-314)

The crisis hit a critical point in September 2008 with the failure, buyout or bailout of the largest entities in the U.S. [shadow banking system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_banking_system "Shadow banking system"). Investment bank [Lehman Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehman_Brothers "Lehman Brothers") failed, while [Merrill Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_Lynch "Merrill Lynch") was purchased by [Bank of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_America "Bank of America"). Investment banks [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs") and [Morgan Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley") obtained depository bank holding charters, which gave them access to emergency lines of credit from the Federal Reserve.[[315]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-315) Government-sponsored enterprises [Fannie Mae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fannie_Mae "Fannie Mae") and [Freddie Mac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mac "Freddie Mac") were taken over by the federal government. Insurance giant [AIG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIG "AIG"), which had sold insurance-like protection for mortgage-backed securities, did not have the capital to honor its commitments; U.S. taxpayers covered its obligations instead in a bailout that exceeded $100 billion.[[316]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-316)

Further, there was the equivalent of a [bank run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_run "Bank run") on other parts of the shadow system, which severely disrupted the ability of non-financial institutions to obtain the funds to run their daily operations. During a one-week period in September 2008, $170 billion (~$242 billion in 2024) were withdrawn from US [money funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_fund "Money fund"), causing the Federal Reserve to announce that it would guarantee these funds up to a point.[[317]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-317) The money market had been a key source of credit for banks ([CDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certificate_of_deposit "Certificate of deposit")) and nonfinancial firms ([commercial paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_paper "Commercial paper")). The [TED spread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TED_spread "TED spread") (see graph above), a measure of the risk of interbank lending, quadrupled shortly after the Lehman failure. This credit freeze brought the global financial system to the brink of collapse.

In a meeting on September 18, 2008, Treasury Secretary [Henry Paulson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Paulson "Henry Paulson") and Fed Chairman [Ben Bernanke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Bernanke "Ben Bernanke") met with key legislators to propose a $700 billion (~$998 billion in 2024) emergency bailout of the banking system. Bernanke reportedly told them: "If we don't do this, we may not have an economy on Monday."[[318]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-318) The [Emergency Economic Stabilization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_Economic_Stabilization_Act "Emergency Economic Stabilization Act"), also called the [Troubled Asset Relief Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troubled_Asset_Relief_Program "Troubled Asset Relief Program") (TARP), was signed into law on October 3, 2008.[[319]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-Associated_Press-Raum-2008-10-03-319)

In a nine-day period from October 1–9, the [S&P 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S&P_500 "S&P 500") fell a staggering 251 points, losing 21.6% of its value.[[320]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-320) The week of October 6–10 saw the largest percentage drop in the history of the [Dow Jones Industrial Average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dow_Jones_Industrial_Average "Dow Jones Industrial Average") – even worse than any single week in the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression").[[321]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-321)

The response of the US [Federal Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve "Federal Reserve"), the [European Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank "European Central Bank"), and other central banks was dramatic. During the last quarter of 2008, these central banks purchased US$2.5 (~$3.57 trillion in 2024) trillion of government debt and troubled private assets from banks. This was the largest liquidity injection into the credit market, and the largest monetary policy action, in world history. The governments of European nations and the US also raised the capital of their national banking systems by $1.5 trillion, by purchasing newly issued [preferred stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preferred_stock "Preferred stock") in their major banks.[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-foreignaffairs1-314) On December 16, 2008, the Federal Reserve cut the [Federal funds rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_funds_rate "Federal funds rate") to 0–0.25%, where it remained until December 2015; this period of [zero interest-rate policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_interest-rate_policy "Zero interest-rate policy") was unprecedented in U.S. history.[[322]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-322)

The International Monetary Fund estimated that large U.S. and European banks lost more than $1 trillion on toxic assets and from bad loans from January 2007 to September 2009. These losses were expected to top $2.8 trillion from 2007 to 2010. U.S. banks losses were forecast to hit $1 trillion and European bank losses will reach $1.6 trillion. The IMF estimated that U.S. banks were about 60 through their losses, but British and eurozone banks only 40%.[[323]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subprime_mortgage_crisis#cite_note-323)
